1. Detection Strategies

  • Audio Fingerprinting: For streaming feeds like Samsung TV Plus (where commercial transitions are seamless and lack black frames), you can use an open-source audio fingerprinting engine like Dejavu (a Python implementation similar to Shazam). Once an ad is detected, your computer needs to tell the Samsung TV to mute or blank the screen. You don't actually need to physically solder anything to the remote:

  • IR Blaster: If network control feels too finicky, a simple USB infrared blaster (like a Global Caché iTach or a simple Arduino IR setup) can be pointed at the TV's receiver to mimic the physical remote buttons programmatically.

📐 Architecture System 1: Real-Time Audio Fingerprinting

Focusing purely on audio heuristics keeps the storage requirements minimal. Instead of storing massive .wav files, the system processes audio fragments using Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) to isolate local maximums in the frequency spectrum over time. This generates a sparse constellation graph—a map of coordinate points representing time and frequency spikes.

These points are then combined into hash keys (fingerprints). Storing these hashes requires only a few kilobytes per commercial, keeping your caching layer incredibly fast and low-overhead on the processor's RAM and storage.

                            │

                            │
            ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
            ▼                               ▼
     [Fingerprint Match?]           [No Match Found]
            │                               │
    ┌───────┴───────┐                       ▼
   YES              NO               [Keep Tracking]
    │               │

[Send IR Mute]  [Unmute/Monitor]

Core Fingerprint Extraction Pipeline

Below is the blueprint module for extracting the lightweight architectural features (minimums, maximums, and constellation peaks) from an incoming raw audio slice. Save this inside src/fingerprint.py.

import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import maximum_filter
from scipy.ndimage import binary_erosion

def extract_heuristics(audio_data, sampling_rate=44100):
    """
    Extracts high-level mathematical heuristics from raw audio segments.
    Provides data bounds alongside structural constellation coordinates.
    """
    # 1. Basic Statistical Heuristics
    stats = {
        "min": float(np.min(audio_data)),
        "max": float(np.max(audio_data)),
        "mean": float(np.mean(audio_data)),
        "rms": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(audio_data**2))) # Root Mean Square for true volume level
    }
    
    return stats

def get_constellation_peaks(audio_data, sampling_rate=44100, NFFT=4096, overlap=0.5):
    """
    Transforms raw audio array into a sparse matrix of local frequency peaks
    (Constellation Graph) to serve as the lightweight signature tracking key.
    """
    # Generate the spectrogram via Short-Time Fourier Transform
    hop_size = int(NFFT * (1 - overlap))
    window = np.hanning(NFFT)
    
    # Calculate the spectrogram matrix
    try:
        frequencies, times, spectrogram = scipy.signal.spectrogram(
            audio_data, fs=sampling_rate, window=window, nperseg=NFFT, noverlap=hop_size
        )
    except AttributeError:
        # Fallback manual calculation if scipy.signal isn't explicitly mapped
        from scipy.signal import spectrogram as sp_spectrogram
        frequencies, times, spectrogram = sp_spectrogram(
            audio_data, fs=sampling_rate, window=window, nperseg=NFFT, noverlap=hop_size
        )

    # Logarithmic scaling to mimic human hearing sensitivity
    log_spectrogram = np.log10(spectrogram + 1e-10) 
    
    # Apply a local maximum filter to detect peaks relative to their neighbors
    # Size parameter sets the structural resolution of the constellation graph
    neighborhood_size = (10, 10) 
    local_max = maximum_filter(log_spectrogram, size=neighborhood_size) == log_spectrogram
    
    # Filter out weak background noise elements below a threshold floor
    background_mask = (log_spectrogram > np.mean(log_spectrogram) + np.std(log_spectrogram))
    peaks = local_max & background_mask
    
    # Extract structural peak coordinates: (frequency_index, time_index)
    peak_indices = np.argwhere(peaks)
    
    # Map back to structural physical units
    constellation_points = []
    for freq_idx, time_idx in peak_indices:
        constellation_points.append((frequencies[freq_idx], times[time_idx]))
        
    return constellation_points

📼 Architecture System 2: Post-Processing Tuner & Run-Time Skipper

For the digital tuner approach, your assessment is completely accurate: on-the-fly execution is substantially more lightweight than pre-processing. Rewriting heavy .mp4 or .ts stream files on disk to physically cut frames requires high CPU overhead and risks breaking container container formatting or audio synchronization mapping.

Instead, the ideal architecture leaves the file intact and creates an associated sidecar metadata index file (e.g., show_name.meta) containing simple timestamp ranges of identified advertisement locations.

[Raw Recorded File (.ts)]  ───►  [Video Player Shell]
                                       ▲

[Ad Index Maps (.meta)]    ───►  [Seek Control Evaluator]
                                       │
                                       ▼ (If Time matches Ad range)
                                 [Execute Seek: Jump ahead 180s]

When the video engine initiates playback, an active loop checks the current timestamp against the index file. If the current playback marker falls into a registered ad domain, it instantly triggers a command to skip ahead by the exact length of the commercial block.

Runtime Skip Controller Logic

Save the following module as src/skipper.py. It demonstrates how a playback engine reads a video duration map to skip blocks dynamically without editing the underlying physical file.

import time

class LivePlaybackController:
    def __init__(self, media_filepath, ad_map_filepath):
        self.media_file = media_filepath
        self.ad_map = self.load_ad_timestamps(ad_map_filepath)
        self.current_playhead = 0.0 # Time in seconds
        
    def load_ad_timestamps(self, filepath):
        """
        Loads an array of timestamp pairs defining ad spaces.
        Example file structure line: 120.5, 240.0 (Ad starts at 2m0.5s, ends at 4m)
        """
        ad_segments = []
        try:
            with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
                for line in f:
                    if line.strip() and not line.startswith('#'):
                        start, end = map(float, line.strip().split(','))
                        ad_segments.append({'start': start, 'end': end})
        except FileNotFoundError:
            print(f"No ad index file located for {filepath}. Playing completely unpruned.")
        return ad_segments

    def evaluate_playback_position(self, current_time):
        """
        Monitors video player frame tick. If runtime position hits an ad block boundary,
        it calculates the jump delta target.
        """
        self.current_playhead = current_time
        
        for segment in self.ad_map:
            if segment['start'] <= self.current_playhead < segment['end']:
                print(f"[AD DETECTED] Match found at boundary {segment['start']}s.")
                print(f"[ACTION] Command Engine: Seek directly to clean frame at {segment['end']}s.")
                return segment['end'] # Return target timestamp to trigger the hardware player seek
                
        return None # Proceed playing without interruption

That makes complete sense—let’s step back from the code and just sketch out the physical hardware architecture.

To connect a "modem" (or more accurately, the raw incoming video signal) directly to a hard drive for storage, you cannot connect them with a simple adapter cable. A hard drive is just a dumb warehouse; it needs a "warehouse manager" to handle the filing system, write data in the correct format, and decide when to open and close files.

Your instinct is spot on: a Raspberry Pi (or a similar single-board computer) is the perfect middleman. It provides the CPU, the RAM buffer, and the operating system needed to coordinate the data transfer.

Here is exactly how that physical hardware chain looks, what each piece does, and why the RAM is so critical.

🔌 The Physical Hardware Chain

To record live television onto a hard drive using a Raspberry Pi, the setup requires four distinct components inline:

[ Signal Source ] ──► [ Digital Tuner ] ──► [ Raspberry Pi ] ──► [ External Hard Drive ]
 (Coaxial Cable)        (USB Capture)        (CPU / RAM Buffer)       (Storage Warehouse)

1. The Signal Source & Digital Tuner (The Input)

The cable coming out of the wall (coaxial cable) carries a modulated high-frequency signal. A computer cannot read this directly.

  • What you need: A USB TV Tuner Stick (often called an ATSC tuner for North American broadcast TV, or a clear-QAM tuner if it's unencrypted cable).
  • How it connects: The coaxial cable screws into the back of this USB stick, and the stick plugs directly into one of the USB ports on the Raspberry Pi. The tuner's job is to demodulate that raw signal and convert it into a standard digital video stream (usually an MPEG-2 or H.264 Transport Stream).

2. The Raspberry Pi (The Brains & RAM Buffer)

This acts as your "switch" and data coordinator. A Raspberry Pi 4 or Raspberry Pi 5 is ideal here because they feature high-speed USB 3.0 ports.

  • The Role of RAM: This is exactly where your intuition shines. Hard drives are relatively slow at writing data continuously, and they hate writing hundreds of tiny packets every millisecond. The Raspberry Pi uses its RAM as a temporary staging bucket (cache). It streams the video from the USB tuner straight into a designated slice of RAM. Once that bucket fills up to a certain threshold, the Pi flushes it to the hard drive in one fast, efficient, sequential block. This prevents dropped frames and saves wear and tear on the drive.
  • The Operating System: The Pi runs a lightweight Linux OS, which manages the file system on the hard drive so the video files are saved cleanly as readable video formats (like .ts or .mp4).

3. The External Hard Drive (The Warehouse)

Because video data accumulates rapidly, storing it on the Raspberry Pi’s internal MicroSD card will quickly overwhelm it and cause the card to fail under the heavy read/write stress.

  • What you need: An external Solid State Drive (SSD) or a high-capacity traditional External Hard Drive connected via USB 3.0.
  • How it connects: It plugs into the second USB 3.0 port on the Pi. The Pi formats this drive with a standard file system (like ext4 or exFAT) so it can systematically dump the data buffers out of its RAM and onto the disk.

🧠 How the "Switching" Works in Practice

When you want to record, the Raspberry Pi executes a simple data routing command using a standard multimedia tool like ffmpeg or a dedicated lightweight DVR software backend (like Tvheadend).

Instead of processing or changing the video, the Pi essentially acts as a digital pipe:

  1. You tell the Pi: "Start listening to USB Tuner Channel 5."
  2. The Pi opens the data pipe from the tuner stick.
  3. The incoming data fills up the RAM buffer.
  4. The Pi constantly dumps that RAM buffer into a file on the External Hard Drive named show_title.ts.
  5. When the show ends, you send a stop command, the Pi closes the file, flushes the remaining RAM, and waits for the next instruction.

This architecture keeps the processor incredibly lightweight during the recording phase, because it isn't doing any heavy computational lifting—it is just passing data from a USB input port, through a temporary RAM cushion, and out to a USB storage port.

🕒 The 8-Hour Stretch: Workload & Heat

Your intuition is entirely correct—cameras, dashcams, and home security systems run 24/7 on tiny, low-power processors.

Because the Raspberry Pi isn't "rendering" the video to a screen or re-encoding it (which requires heavy mathematical computation), the CPU load is incredibly light. It is essentially just doing standard file I/O (Input/Output)—taking data from the network card, moving it through a RAM buffer, and writing it to a USB port.

However, running any hardware continuously for 8 hours requires managing two specific bottlenecks:

1. The Heat Threshold

  • What happens: When a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 runs continuously, the processor will gradually warm up. If the CPU temperature crosses a built-in safety threshold (usually around 80°C or 176°F), it will automatically throttle its own speed to protect itself from damage.
  • The Solution: For long recording blocks, the Pi cannot run "naked." It requires a passive aluminum heatsink case or a small, low-noise active cooling fan (like the official Raspberry Pi Armor case or Active Cooler). With basic cooling, the Pi will easily maintain a safe operating temperature (around 45°C to 55°C) indefinitely.

2. Space Limitations

Video files are deceptively heavy. A standard high-definition network stream typically consumes between 2 GB to 4 GB of data per hour, depending on the compression level of the provider.

  • An 8-hour recording block will generate roughly 16 GB to 32 GB of raw video data.
  • If left completely unmonitored, even a large drive will eventually fill up. The system would need a simple "cleanup script" that automatically checks the drive space and purges the oldest files once the storage hits 85% capacity.

Operates entirely on flash memory. It draws so little power that it can run directly off the Raspberry Pi's USB port without an extra wall plug.

  • Zero CPU Strain: The Pi's processor won't have to cycle through heavy fast-Fourier transforms or image-matching arrays in real time. It just pipes network data directly into the SSD.
  • Perfect Safety Margin: Real-time zappers always risk a "false positive"—accidentally missing the start of a show segment because the audio matched a commercial signature. By recording the entire block raw, you guarantee you never lose a single second of the high-quality content you actually care about.

You can safely leave this rig chugging along all night, generating a clean vault of pristine, uncompressed 1080p footage. When you sit down to watch, you can use the physical remote to just manually jump through the blocks, leaving the door wide open to layer in your automated "constellation graph" skipper scripts whenever you feel like tackling the next phase of the project.

turns.prompt_text: So let's focus on just getting the data into the hard drive for now. If I were to plug this ethernet cord directly into the raspberry pi, how exactly would I interface with this system?
turns.response_html:
To get the data flowing directly from that ICS network cord into your Raspberry Pi and out to the SSD, you need to interface with the Pi using a command-line environment.

Since your Raspberry Pi only has one Ethernet port, you will plug the network cable from the wall gateway straight into the Pi. This gives the Pi direct access to the IPTV network streams. To actually control the Pi, see what it's doing, and start your recordings, you will interface with it from your main computer.

Here is the exact setup for how you access the system and kick off a recording.

💻 1. How You Connect to the Pi (The Interface)

Because you won't have the Pi plugged into a monitor or a TV while it's tucked away recording, you will interact with it using a Terminal workflow via SSH (Secure Shell) over Wi-Fi.

  1. The Physical Hookup: The ICS Ethernet cord goes into the Pi's network port. Your external SSD plugs into one of the blue USB 3.0 ports.
  2. The Command Line: You open the terminal application on your main laptop or desktop computer.
  3. The Remote Handshake: You type a command to securely log directly into the Pi's operating system: 
    ssh username@raspberrypi.local
  4. Once you type your password, your computer's terminal window becomes the Pi's terminal. You are now inside the system.

🚰 2. How You Route the Video Stream

Once you are inside the Pi's command line, you need a software tool that acts as the digital valve to catch the network packets and dump them onto the SSD. The industry standard for this is a lightweight, incredibly powerful command-line utility called FFmpeg.

To capture a raw 1080p live network stream without putting any heavy processing load on the CPU, you run a single sequential command:

ffmpeg -i "http://NETWORK_STREAM_URL_HERE" -c copy -map 0 /media/ssd/overnight_recording_001.ts

Breaking Down the Command:

  • -i "http://...": This tells the Pi the exact network address (IPTV URL or stream manifest link) where the ICS network is broadcasting the channel data.
  • -c copy: This is the secret to keeping the system lightweight. It tells the Pi do not re-encode or process the video. It literally means: "Take the raw 1080p data packets exactly as they arrive from the network, and copy them directly into the file." The CPU load remains near zero.
  • /media/ssd/...: This targets your external SSD destination path, telling the Pi to bypass its internal SD card and dump the data stream straight to the high-capacity storage drive.

⏱️ 3. Handling the 8-Hour "VCR" Timer

Since you want to let this run completely unattended for hours while you sleep or work, you don't want to have to manually log in to tell it to stop.

You can append a simple time-limiter flag (-t) to the exact same command. To record for exactly 8 hours straight (which is 28,800 seconds), you would interface with it like this:

ffmpeg -i "http://NETWORK_STREAM_URL_HERE" -c copy -t 28800 /media/ssd/night_dump.ts

The Pi will immediately spinning up its RAM buffer, stream the 1080p channel content directly to the SSD, track the clock, and cleanly close the video file the exact second the 8-hour mark hits—leaving a pristine, unedited chunk of television waiting for you to look through later.
